title: Sourcing and Automation of Political News and Information During Three European Elections
screen_reason: Domain-level content typology applied to the links Twitter users shared under election hashtags in France, the UK and Germany (2017). Table 3 gives, per country, the share of shared links coming from 'Junk News and Information' sources (4.2% / 10.3% / 9.1%) and from the broader 'Divisive and conspiracy sources' category (6.7% / 11.0% / 10.2%). The denominator is links that users shared, so these are SHARING content-shares (per the governing denominator rule: '% of shared links unreliable' is SHARING, not CONTENT).

estimates.date: 13 March 2017 to 19 March 2017 (French presidential election campaign)
estimates.measure_type: % of political news and information links shared in French election-hashtag tweets that came from junk news sources
estimates.denominator: 8,783 coded links shared in French election-hashtag tweets (Table 3 total; the coded sample corresponds to the random 10% of the 88,755 URLs identified in 842,146 French tweets)
estimates.definition: The link's base domain was coded 'Junk News and Information': the source fulfils at least three of five criteria (professionalism, style, credibility, bias, counterfeit)
estimates.misinfo_def: we put forward the concept of "junk news" which we use to refer to sources that publish or aggregate deceptive, conspiratorial, or incorrect information purporting to be real news and political information
estimates.page_loc: Table 3, p. 9, 'Junk News and Information' row - France columns (366 / 4.2 and 586 / 6.7)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Grounded typology built and applied by a team of five language-specific expert coders at the level of the base domain (5,158 web sources labelled; >1,500 hr of coding, six training sessions, bi-weekly review). Junk news = at least 3 of 5 criteria; coders browsed domains for authorship/ownership and corroborated with Wikipedia and third-party fact-checkers (FullFact, Correctiv, AFP Fact Check, Media Bias Fact). Krippendorff's alpha = .89 on the shared English-language US training set; no within-language-team intercoder reliability was computed.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our methodology describes "junk news" as sources that meet three out of the following five criteria: (1) professionalism, where sources fall short of the standards of professional journalistic practice including information about authors, editors, and owners; (2) style, where inflammatory language, suggestion, ad hominem attacks and misleading visuals are used; (3) credibility, where sources report on unsubstantiated claims, rely on conspiratorial and dubious sources, and do not post corrections; (4) bias, where reporting is highly biased and ideologically skewed and opinion is presented as fact; and (5) counterfeit, where sources mimic established news publications in branding, design, and content presentation.
estimates.notes: Percentage is verbatim in Table 3 (366 and 4.2 in the France columns). Denominator note: the paper does not say in so many words what the Table 3 N is; 8,783 is ~9.9% of the 88,755 French URLs, matching 'we prepared a random sample of 10% of tweets for coding', so Table 3 is read as the coded sample with coding decisions later projected to the full dataset. breadth left empty because classification is source-level (domain reliability), not item veracity. denom_selection=curated because the hashtag list was hand-selected (200-300 hashtags reviewed per country) and covers many candidates/parties/issues - a curated multi-hashtag corpus, not a random platform sample; an adjudicator may prefer denom_selection='' with denom_scope=political_news. Note also a within-paper inconsistency in the French tweet total: 843,146 in the text vs 842,146 in Table 1 (does not affect this row). source_quote is the single Table 3 line carrying all three countries; this row reads the France columns (366 / 4.2 and 586 / 6.7). The .txt rendering of this PDF interleaves the two print columns, so only single-line spans are greppable; the moderator_quote, misinfo_def and rob quotes are reconstructed in the paper's reading order (contiguous within one print column, no ellipsis).

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) Amplifier-account figures - 'We identified 92 such accounts that generated 7.4% of the total traffic' (Germany), 16.5% of UK traffic, 7.2% average in France, 16.4% during the French run-off. These describe concentration of ALL political traffic in highly active/automated accounts, not of misinformation exposure or sharing, so they fall outside the review's CONCENTRATION construct; they would also need a computed group share (92/149,573 users) to satisfy R1. (b) The Russia subcategory alone (France 2.5%, UK 0.9%, Germany 1.1%) - reported verbatim in Table 3 and extractable, but it is a narrower slice of the same cell already covered by the junk-news and Divisive-and-Conspiracy rows; left out under R4 to avoid three near-duplicate rows, and it is a state-media/propaganda category rather than a falsity judgement. (c) Ratio statements ('for every one link to Junk News Sources, there were seven links to content produced by professional news organizations'; 5 to 1 in the UK; 4 to 1 in Germany; 2.4 links to political-actor content per divisive link in France) - ratios, not shares with a denominator. (d) Professional-news, political-actor, citizen/civic and 'Other' shares - not misinformation. (e) Party/candidate traffic shares (Table 2) - not misinformation. Uncertainties for the adjudicator: (i) the exact Table 3 denominator is not stated (read as the coded random 10% of URLs per country, which matches the arithmetic); (ii) denom_selection coded 'curated' because the hashtag corpus was hand-selected; (iii) the paper's own text/Table 1 disagree on the French tweet total (843,146 vs 842,146). Quote note: the .txt rendering of this two-column article interleaves the left and right columns line by line, so no multi-line sentence is greppable in the text file. Every source_quote is therefore a single verbatim line of Table 3; the moderator_quote, misinfo_def and rob quotes are reconstructed in the printed reading order (contiguous within a single print column, no ellipsis joins).

rob.design: Twitter Streaming API collection under hand-curated election hashtag sets in three countries (France 842,146 tweets / 88,755 URLs; UK 2,488,804 / 724,988; Germany 984,713 / 115,563); no probability sample of users and Streaming API caps at ~1% of global public tweets (limitation acknowledged); tweets without hashtags not captured; random 10% of tweets coded and domain-level decisions projected to the full dataset; grounded typology applied to 5,158 base domains by five language-specific expert coders, >1,500 hr of coding, six training sessions; Krippendorff's alpha = .89 measured only on the shared English-language US training set, with no within-language-team reliability computed; disagreements resolved in face-to-face meetings; no veracity assessment of individual stories.
rob.item6_quote: Our methodology describes "junk news" as sources that meet three out of the following five criteria: (1) professionalism, where sources fall short of the standards of professional journalistic practice including information about authors, editors, and owners; (2) style, where inflammatory language, suggestion, ad hominem attacks and misleading visuals are used; (3) credibility, where sources report on unsubstantiated claims, rely on conspiratorial and dubious sources, and do not post corrections; (4) bias, where reporting is highly biased and ideologically skewed and opinion is presented as fact; and (5) counterfeit, where sources mimic established news publications in branding, design, and content presentation.
